about: Homeostasis is a Part IA subject of the Cambridge Medical and Veterinary Sciences Tripos covering the physiological systems that keep the body's internal environment stable: nerve function, neuromuscular transmission, muscle, circulation, respiration, excretion and water balance, digestion and absorption, metabolism and thermoregulation, with practical classes in experimental physiology and histology. It is examined together with Histology. The Faculty's (undated) examination table lists a 1-hour section on lecture material (MCQs or short notes), two 1-hour MCQ sections on practical work and a 2-hour essay section that counts for the Tripos but not the 2nd MB. In 2023-24 these were 60 theory MCQs, 40 experimental-practical MCQs, 30 histology MCQs and two essays chosen from five; check the current year's arrangements. The University's regulations also require practical notebooks. No published lecture-by-lecture order was available, so the topics below follow the subject list in the course description and regulations.

notes.body:
Every cell has a voltage across its membrane. In nerve and muscle this voltage can change rapidly, carrying signals. Homeostasis starts with how these potentials arise.

Ion gradients (typical mammalian values)
- K⁺: about 140 mM inside, 4–5 mM outside.
- Na⁺: about 10–15 mM inside, about 145 mM outside.
- Cl⁻: low inside (varies by cell), about 110 mM outside.
- Ca²⁺: about 100 nM free inside, about 1–2 mM outside.
The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pumps 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in per ATP. It maintains the gradients and is electrogenic, but its direct contribution to the resting potential is only a few mV.

Equilibrium potentials: the Nernst equation
E = (RT/zF) ln([ion]out/[ion]in). At 37 °C this is about (61.5/z) × log₁₀([out]/[in]) mV.
- Worked example: E_K = 61.5 × log₁₀(4.5/140) = 61.5 × (−1.49) ≈ −92 mV.
- E_Na = 61.5 × log₁₀(145/12) ≈ +66 mV.

The resting membrane potential
- About −70 mV in many neurons and about −90 mV in skeletal muscle.
- At rest the membrane is far more permeable to K⁺ (through leak channels) than to Na⁺, so the resting potential lies close to E_K but slightly less negative because of a small Na⁺ leak.
- The Goldman–Hodgkin–Katz equation weights each ion's concentrations by its permeability; the potential moves towards the equilibrium potential of whichever ion is most permeant.
- Clinical link: raised plasma K⁺ (hyperkalaemia) makes E_K less negative and depolarises cells. This inactivates Na⁺ channels and can cause dangerous cardiac arrhythmias.

The action potential
Hodgkin and Huxley worked out its ionic basis in the squid giant axon (published 1952).
- A stimulus depolarises the membrane to threshold (roughly −55 mV).
- Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open; Na⁺ entry depolarises further, opening more channels (positive feedback). The membrane overshoots to about +30 to +40 mV, approaching E_Na.
- Na⁺ channels inactivate within about a millisecond.
- Voltage-gated K⁺ channels open more slowly; K⁺ efflux repolarises the membrane, often producing an afterhyperpolarisation.
- Absolute refractory period: no second action potential is possible (Na⁺ channels inactivated). Relative refractory period: a stronger stimulus is needed.
- Action potentials are all-or-none; stimulus intensity is coded by firing frequency.

Conduction along axons
- Local circuit currents spread passively ahead of the active region and depolarise the next segment to threshold. Refractoriness behind the impulse keeps it travelling one way.
- Passive spread depends on the length constant λ = √(r_m/r_i): it is greater when membrane resistance is high and internal resistance is low.
- Larger diameter lowers internal resistance and speeds conduction.
- Myelin (Schwann cells peripherally, oligodendrocytes centrally) raises membrane resistance and lowers capacitance, so the impulse jumps between nodes of Ranvier, where Na⁺ channels cluster: saltatory conduction.
- Large myelinated motor fibres conduct at up to around 100 m/s; small unmyelinated C fibres at about 1 m/s.
- Demyelination slows or blocks conduction: multiple sclerosis (central) and Guillain–Barré syndrome (peripheral).
- Local anaesthetics block voltage-gated Na⁺ channels, preventing action potentials in sensory fibres.

Exam tips: be ready to calculate a Nernst potential, explain why the resting potential is near E_K, and link channel behaviour to each phase of the action potential and the refractory period.

notes.h: Neuromuscular transmission and the autonomic nervous system
notes.body:
Synapses convert electrical signals into chemical ones and back. The neuromuscular junction (NMJ) is the best-understood example, and the autonomic nervous system uses similar mechanisms to control internal organs.

Steps at the neuromuscular junction
- An action potential reaches the motor nerve terminal.
- Voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels open and Ca²⁺ enters.
- Ca²⁺ triggers fusion of acetylcholine (ACh)-containing vesicles with the membrane, via SNARE proteins, releasing ACh into the cleft.
- ACh binds nicotinic receptors on the motor end-plate. These are ligand-gated cation channels letting Na⁺ in and K⁺ out, so they depolarise the end-plate (the end-plate potential, EPP).
- The EPP normally far exceeds threshold (a high safety factor), so it triggers an action potential in the muscle fibre through voltage-gated Na⁺ channels.
- Acetylcholinesterase in the cleft rapidly hydrolyses ACh to choline and acetate; choline is taken back up to make new ACh.

Quantal release
Bernard Katz and colleagues showed in the 1950s that ACh is released in packets (quanta), each producing a small miniature end-plate potential even without nerve stimulation. A nerve impulse releases many quanta at once.

Clinical and pharmacological links
- Myasthenia gravis: autoantibodies against nicotinic ACh receptors reduce the EPP, causing fatigable weakness (often eyelids and eye muscles first). Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors improve symptoms by prolonging ACh action.
- Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome: antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels, often associated with small-cell lung cancer; strength may briefly improve with repeated effort.
- Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins and blocks ACh release, causing flaccid paralysis.
- Non-depolarising blockers (e.g. tubocurarine, derived from curare) compete with ACh at nicotinic receptors. Suxamethonium is a depolarising blocker.
- Organophosphates irreversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase, causing excessive cholinergic stimulation.

The autonomic nervous system (ANS)
Two-neuron pathway: a preganglionic neuron from the CNS synapses in a ganglion with a postganglionic neuron that reaches the target.

Sympathetic division
- Thoracolumbar outflow (T1 to L2).
- Short preganglionic fibres to paravertebral or prevertebral ganglia; long postganglionic fibres.
- Ganglionic transmitter: ACh on nicotinic receptors. Postganglionic transmitter: mostly noradrenaline on adrenoceptors.
- Exceptions: sweat glands receive sympathetic cholinergic fibres (muscarinic receptors). The adrenal medulla is innervated directly by preganglionic fibres and releases mainly adrenaline, plus noradrenaline, into the blood.

Parasympathetic division
- Craniosacral outflow (cranial nerves III, VII, IX and X; sacral segments S2 to S4). The vagus nerve supplies most thoracic and abdominal organs.
- Long preganglionic fibres to ganglia in or near the target; short postganglionic fibres.
- ACh at both synapses: nicotinic in ganglia, muscarinic on target cells.

Receptors and typical effects
- α1: vasoconstriction, contraction of the radial (dilator) muscle of the iris.
- α2: presynaptic inhibition of noradrenaline release.
- β1: increased heart rate and contractility; renin release.
- β2: bronchodilation, vasodilation in skeletal muscle, relaxation of uterine smooth muscle.
- M2 (heart): slows the heart. M3 (smooth muscle and glands): bronchoconstriction, gut motility and secretion, bladder detrusor contraction, constriction of the pupil.

Organ effects
- Heart: sympathetic increases rate and force; parasympathetic (vagal) slows the rate.
- Pupil: sympathetic dilates; parasympathetic constricts.
- Bronchi: sympathetic (mainly via circulating adrenaline on β2) dilates; parasympathetic constricts and increases mucus.
- Gut: parasympathetic increases motility and secretion; sympathetic reduces them.
- Bladder: parasympathetic contracts the detrusor (voiding).
Most organs receive both divisions, but most blood vessels receive only sympathetic fibres.

Autonomic nerves release transmitter from varicosities along their terminals, and co-transmitters such as ATP, neuropeptide Y, VIP and nitric oxide also contribute.

Exam tips: draw the NMJ sequence from nerve action potential to muscle action potential, and learn the transmitter and receptor at each autonomic synapse, including the exceptions.

All three muscle types contract by myosin pulling on actin, powered by ATP and switched on by Ca²⁺. They differ in structure, how Ca²⁺ is delivered and how contraction is regulated.

Skeletal muscle structure
- Fibres are long multinucleate cells containing myofibrils made of repeating sarcomeres (Z line to Z line).
- Thin filaments: actin with tropomyosin and troponin. Thick filaments: myosin.
- A band (length of thick filaments) stays constant during contraction; the I band and H zone shorten. This observation underpinned the sliding filament theory (proposed in 1954 by A. F. Huxley and Niedergerke, and by H. E. Huxley and Hanson).

The cross-bridge cycle
- ATP binds myosin, which detaches from actin.
- ATP is hydrolysed, "cocking" the myosin head.
- The head binds actin; release of phosphate triggers the power stroke; ADP is released.
- Without ATP, heads stay attached: rigor (as in rigor mortis).

Excitation–contraction coupling in skeletal muscle
- The action potential travels down transverse (T) tubules.
- Dihydropyridine receptors (voltage-sensing L-type Ca²⁺ channels) in the T-tubule are mechanically linked to ryanodine receptors (RyR1) on the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR), which release Ca²⁺.
- Ca²⁺ binds troponin C, moving tropomyosin off the myosin-binding sites on actin.
- Relaxation: the SR Ca²⁺-ATPase (SERCA) pumps Ca²⁺ back into the SR.
- Malignant hyperthermia: inherited RyR1 mutations can cause uncontrolled Ca²⁺ release when exposed to some anaesthetic agents, producing a dangerous rise in temperature.

Grading force in skeletal muscle
- A single action potential gives a twitch. Repeated stimulation before relaxation gives summation; high-frequency stimulation gives a fused tetanus.
- Motor units (a motor neuron and the fibres it supplies) are recruited from small to large as force increases (the size principle).
- Length–tension relationship: force is maximal at an intermediate sarcomere length where filament overlap is optimal.
- Fibre types: type I (slow, oxidative, fatigue-resistant), type IIa (fast, oxidative and glycolytic) and type IIx (fast, glycolytic, fatigable).

Cardiac muscle
- Striated, with sarcomeres, but cells are branched, usually single-nucleated, and joined by intercalated discs containing gap junctions, so the myocardium behaves as an electrical syncytium.
- Ca²⁺-induced Ca²⁺ release: Ca²⁺ entering through L-type channels during the plateau triggers further release from the SR via RyR2.
- The long plateau and refractory period mean the heart cannot be tetanised, so it always relaxes and refills.
- Force is varied by changing Ca²⁺ handling (contractility) and by stretch (Frank–Starling mechanism), not by recruiting motor units.

Smooth muscle
- No sarcomeres: actin filaments attach to dense bodies, so cells look unstriated.
- Ca²⁺ comes from outside the cell (through voltage-gated and receptor-operated channels) and from the SR (via IP₃ receptors).
- Ca²⁺ binds calmodulin, which activates myosin light-chain kinase (MLCK). MLCK phosphorylates the myosin regulatory light chain, allowing cross-bridge cycling.
- Myosin light-chain phosphatase dephosphorylates it, causing relaxation. Changing the balance of kinase and phosphatase alters sensitivity to Ca²⁺.
- Contraction is slow and economical; the "latch" state maintains tone at low ATP cost.
- Single-unit (visceral) smooth muscle, as in the gut, uterus and bladder, is coupled by gap junctions and often shows spontaneous pacemaker activity. Multi-unit smooth muscle, as in the iris and large airways, is controlled more by individual nerve fibres.

Exam tips: compare the three muscle types in a table (structure, Ca²⁺ source, Ca²⁺ sensor, how force is graded, nervous control). MCQs often test troponin versus calmodulin and DHP–RyR1 coupling versus Ca²⁺-induced Ca²⁺ release.

The heart is two pumps in series, driven by its own electrical system and adjusted by nerves, hormones and the filling pressure.

The conducting system
- The sinoatrial (SA) node in the right atrium is the normal pacemaker.
- The impulse spreads across the atria to the atrioventricular (AV) node, which delays it (about 0.1 s) so the atria can finish emptying.
- It then passes through the bundle of His, the left and right bundle branches and the Purkinje fibres, which spread excitation rapidly through the ventricles from apex towards base.

Pacemaker potential (SA node)
- No stable resting potential. Slow diastolic depolarisation is produced partly by the "funny" current (I_f, an inward Na⁺-carrying current through HCN channels, activated by hyperpolarisation), together with Ca²⁺ currents and declining K⁺ current.
- The upstroke is produced by L-type Ca²⁺ channels, not fast Na⁺ channels, so it is slow.
- Sympathetic stimulation (β1, raising cAMP) increases I_f and Ca²⁺ current and speeds the rate. Vagal stimulation (M2) opens K⁺ channels and reduces I_f, slowing the rate. At rest vagal tone dominates: the intrinsic SA node rate is higher than the normal resting heart rate.

Ventricular action potential
- Phase 0: rapid depolarisation through fast Na⁺ channels.
- Phase 1: brief partial repolarisation (transient outward K⁺ current).
- Phase 2: plateau, with Ca²⁺ entry through L-type channels balanced by K⁺ exit.
- Phase 3: repolarisation as K⁺ currents dominate.
- Phase 4: stable resting potential.
The plateau makes the refractory period nearly as long as contraction, preventing tetanus.

The ECG
- P wave: atrial depolarisation.
- QRS complex: ventricular depolarisation (normally under 0.12 s).
- T wave: ventricular repolarisation.
- PR interval (normally 0.12–0.20 s) reflects mainly AV nodal delay.

The cardiac cycle
- Ventricular filling during diastole (mostly passive; atrial contraction adds the final portion).
- Isovolumetric contraction: AV valves close (first heart sound), all valves shut, pressure rises.
- Ejection: semilunar valves open when ventricular pressure exceeds arterial pressure.
- Isovolumetric relaxation: semilunar valves close (second heart sound).

Cardiac output
- CO = heart rate × stroke volume. Example: 70 beats/min × 70 mL ≈ 4.9 L/min.
- Stroke volume = end-diastolic volume (EDV) − end-systolic volume (ESV).
- Ejection fraction = SV/EDV. Example: EDV 120 mL, ESV 50 mL gives SV 70 mL and EF ≈ 58% (normal is roughly 55–70%).

Determinants of stroke volume
- Preload (end-diastolic stretch): the Frank–Starling law states that greater filling produces a more forceful contraction and larger stroke volume. This automatically matches the outputs of the two ventricles. Mechanisms include better filament overlap and increased Ca²⁺ sensitivity of the myofilaments at longer lengths.
- Contractility (inotropy): force at a given preload. Sympathetic β1 stimulation raises cAMP, activating protein kinase A, which increases Ca²⁺ entry through L-type channels and speeds Ca²⁺ re-uptake (by phosphorylating phospholamban). Contraction becomes stronger and relaxation faster.
- Afterload: the load against which the ventricle ejects, related to arterial pressure; higher afterload reduces stroke volume.

Coronary circulation
- The heart extracts a large proportion of the oxygen delivered to it even at rest, so greater demand is met mainly by increasing coronary flow (metabolic vasodilation).
- Flow to the left ventricle occurs mainly in diastole, because contraction compresses intramyocardial vessels. Fast heart rates shorten diastole and can compromise perfusion.

Exam tips: be able to draw and label a Wiggers diagram (pressures, volumes, ECG and heart sounds) and explain how sympathetic and vagal activity alter rate and force at the ion-channel level.

The circulation delivers flow to tissues according to their needs while keeping arterial pressure fairly stable.

Pressure, flow and resistance
- Flow = pressure difference ÷ resistance. Applied to the whole systemic circulation: mean arterial pressure (MAP) ≈ cardiac output × total peripheral resistance (assuming central venous pressure is near zero).
- MAP ≈ diastolic pressure + one-third of pulse pressure. Example: 120/80 mmHg gives MAP ≈ 80 + 40/3 ≈ 93 mmHg.
- Poiseuille's law: resistance = 8ηL/(πr⁴). Resistance is inversely proportional to the fourth power of radius, so halving vessel radius increases resistance 16-fold. Small changes in arteriolar diameter therefore control flow powerfully.

Functions of different vessels
- Elastic arteries damp pressure pulses; arterioles are the main resistance vessels; capillaries have the largest total cross-sectional area and slowest flow, ideal for exchange; veins are capacitance vessels holding most of the blood volume.

Capillary exchange: Starling forces
- Net filtration = K_f [(P_c − P_i) − σ(π_c − π_i)], where P is hydrostatic pressure, π is oncotic pressure, c is capillary and i is interstitium, and σ is the reflection coefficient for protein.
- The classic teaching is filtration at the arterial end and reabsorption at the venous end. The revised Starling principle, which emphasises the endothelial glycocalyx, holds that in most tissues there is little sustained reabsorption at steady state, and lymph returns most filtered fluid. Textbooks differ, so state which model you are using.
- Oedema results from raised capillary pressure (e.g. heart failure, venous obstruction), low plasma oncotic pressure (low albumin, e.g. nephrotic syndrome, liver failure), increased permeability (inflammation) or lymphatic obstruction.

Local control of blood flow
- Myogenic response (described by Bayliss): arteriolar smooth muscle contracts when stretched, contributing to autoregulation of flow in organs such as the brain and kidney.
- Metabolic control: falling O₂ and rising CO₂, H⁺, K⁺ and adenosine dilate arterioles (active hyperaemia during exercise; reactive hyperaemia after occlusion).
- Endothelium: nitric oxide (from endothelial NO synthase, stimulated by shear stress and some agonists) relaxes smooth muscle via cGMP; endothelin constricts.

Short-term control: the baroreceptor reflex
- Stretch receptors in the carotid sinus (afferents in the glossopharyngeal nerve, IX) and aortic arch (vagus, X) increase firing as pressure rises.
- Afferents project to the nucleus tractus solitarius in the medulla.
- A rise in pressure increases vagal outflow and reduces sympathetic outflow: heart rate, contractility and peripheral resistance fall, and venous capacitance increases. A fall in pressure does the opposite.
- Standing up: blood pools in the legs, venous return and stroke volume fall, and arterial pressure dips. The baroreflex raises heart rate and resistance within seconds. Failure causes postural (orthostatic) hypotension.
- Baroreceptors reset to a new level if pressure stays high, so they mainly buffer short-term changes.

Long-term control: the kidney and blood volume
- Pressure natriuresis: higher arterial pressure increases renal Na⁺ and water excretion, reducing volume.
- Renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system: low renal perfusion pressure, sympathetic (β1) activity and low NaCl delivery to the macula densa stimulate renin release. Angiotensin II constricts arterioles, stimulates aldosterone (Na⁺ retention), ADH release and thirst.
- Antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin) is also released when blood volume falls substantially.
- Atrial natriuretic peptide is released when the atria are stretched and promotes Na⁺ excretion.

Response to haemorrhage
- Immediate: baroreflex causes tachycardia, vasoconstriction (skin, gut, kidney) and venoconstriction, preserving flow to brain and heart.
- Minutes to hours: reduced capillary pressure favours fluid moving into capillaries ("autotransfusion"); RAAS and ADH conserve salt and water; thirst.
- Days to weeks: plasma proteins are replaced by the liver and red cells by increased erythropoietin.

Exam tips: use MAP = CO × TPR to organise any answer on blood pressure, and separate fast neural from slow renal and hormonal mechanisms.

Breathing moves air in and out of the lungs; gas exchange and transport supply O₂ to tissues and remove CO₂; and control systems keep arterial CO₂ and O₂ within narrow limits.

Mechanics of breathing
- Inspiration is active: the diaphragm (phrenic nerve, C3–C5) and external intercostals contract, enlarging the thorax. Intrapleural pressure becomes more negative, the lungs expand and alveolar pressure falls below atmospheric pressure, so air flows in.
- Quiet expiration is passive elastic recoil. Forced expiration uses internal intercostals and abdominal muscles.
- Compliance = change in volume ÷ change in pressure. Low in fibrosis; high in emphysema (loss of elastic tissue).
- Surface tension in alveoli is reduced by surfactant (mainly dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine), secreted by type II alveolar cells. By the law of Laplace (P = 2T/r) small alveoli would otherwise collapse into larger ones. Surfactant deficiency in preterm babies causes neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.
- Airway resistance is mostly in medium-sized bronchi. Bronchoconstriction (e.g. asthma) increases it. Obstructive disease reduces the ratio of FEV₁ to FVC (below about 0.7 is the usual cut-off); restrictive disease reduces both, with a normal or high ratio.

Ventilation
- Tidal volume about 500 mL at rest; anatomical dead space about 150 mL.
- Alveolar ventilation = (tidal volume − dead space) × respiratory rate. Example: (500 − 150) × 12 = 4.2 L/min.
- PaCO₂ is inversely proportional to alveolar ventilation (for a given CO₂ production). Hypoventilation raises PaCO₂; hyperventilation lowers it.

Gas exchange
- Diffusion across the alveolar membrane follows Fick's law: rate ∝ area × partial pressure difference ÷ thickness. It falls in emphysema (less area) and fibrosis (thicker barrier).
- Alveolar gas equation (simplified): PAO₂ = PiO₂ − PaCO₂/R. Breathing air at sea level, PiO₂ ≈ 0.21 × (101.3 − 6.3) ≈ 20 kPa. With PaCO₂ 5.3 kPa and R 0.8, PAO₂ ≈ 20 − 6.6 ≈ 13.3 kPa.
- Ventilation–perfusion (V/Q) mismatch is the commonest cause of hypoxaemia. Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction diverts blood away from poorly ventilated regions.

Oxygen transport
- Most O₂ is carried bound to haemoglobin (about 1.34 mL O₂ per g of fully saturated Hb); a small amount is dissolved.
- The O₂–Hb dissociation curve is sigmoid because binding is cooperative. The flat upper part protects saturation when PO₂ falls a little; the steep part allows O₂ unloading in tissues.
- P₅₀ (PO₂ at 50% saturation) is about 3.5 kPa. The curve shifts right (lower affinity, easier unloading) with raised CO₂, H⁺ (the Bohr effect), temperature and 2,3-BPG. Fetal haemoglobin and carbon monoxide shift it left.

CO₂ transport
- Mostly as bicarbonate (roughly 70%), formed in red cells by carbonic anhydrase; HCO₃⁻ leaves in exchange for Cl⁻ (the chloride shift).
- Some as carbamino compounds with Hb and a small amount dissolved.
- Deoxygenated Hb carries more CO₂ (the Haldane effect), helping CO₂ loading in tissues and unloading in the lungs.

Control of breathing
- Rhythm is generated in the brainstem (medulla, modulated by pontine centres).
- Central chemoreceptors near the ventral surface of the medulla respond to H⁺ in the CSF, which reflects arterial PCO₂ because CO₂ crosses the blood–brain barrier freely. They provide most of the drive from CO₂.
- Peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid bodies via IX, aortic bodies via X) respond mainly to low PaO₂, especially below about 8 kPa, and also to raised PaCO₂ and H⁺. They provide the only response to hypoxia.
- In some people with chronic CO₂ retention, high concentrations of oxygen can raise PaCO₂ further. The traditional explanation (loss of "hypoxic drive") is disputed; worsened V/Q matching through release of hypoxic vasoconstriction and the Haldane effect are thought to contribute substantially.

Exam tips: practise calculations (alveolar ventilation, alveolar gas equation) and be able to explain each shift of the dissociation curve and why it helps tissue O₂ delivery.

notes.h: Kidney, body fluids and water balance
notes.body:
The kidneys regulate the volume and composition of body fluids: water, Na⁺, K⁺, H⁺ and other solutes. They also excrete waste and help control blood pressure.

Body fluid compartments (70 kg adult man)
- Total body water about 60% of body weight (about 42 L): about two-thirds intracellular (about 28 L) and one-third extracellular (about 14 L).
- ECF is roughly three-quarters interstitial fluid and one-quarter plasma (about 3.5 L).
- Plasma osmolality is normally about 285–295 mOsm/kg.

Glomerular filtration
- About 20% of the renal plasma flow is filtered, giving a glomerular filtration rate (GFR) of about 125 mL/min, roughly 180 L/day.
- Filtration is driven by glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure, opposed by Bowman's space pressure and plasma oncotic pressure.
- GFR is autoregulated over a wide range of arterial pressures by the myogenic response and tubuloglomerular feedback (the macula densa senses NaCl delivery and adjusts afferent arteriolar tone).

Clearance
- Clearance C = (U × V)/P, where U is urine concentration, V urine flow and P plasma concentration.
- Inulin is freely filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted, so its clearance equals GFR. Creatinine clearance slightly overestimates GFR because some creatinine is secreted.
- Worked example: U_inulin 30 mg/mL, V 1 mL/min, P 0.25 mg/mL gives C = 30 × 1/0.25 = 120 mL/min.

Tubular function
- Proximal tubule: reabsorbs about two-thirds of filtered Na⁺ and water (isosmotically), nearly all glucose (via SGLT2 and SGLT1) and amino acids, and most bicarbonate. Glucose reabsorption has a transport maximum, so when plasma glucose is very high (as in uncontrolled diabetes) glucose appears in the urine.
- Loop of Henle: the descending limb is permeable to water; the ascending limb is impermeable to water. The thick ascending limb reabsorbs about a quarter of filtered Na⁺ via the Na⁺–K⁺–2Cl⁻ cotransporter (NKCC2), diluting tubular fluid. This drives countercurrent multiplication, which creates a hyperosmotic medulla (up to about 1,200 mOsm/kg in humans). Urea recycling adds to the gradient, and the vasa recta act as countercurrent exchangers that preserve it.
- Distal convoluted tubule: Na⁺–Cl⁻ cotransporter (NCC); regulated Ca²⁺ reabsorption (increased by parathyroid hormone).
- Collecting duct: principal cells reabsorb Na⁺ through ENaC and secrete K⁺, both increased by aldosterone; intercalated cells secrete H⁺ or HCO₃⁻.

Water balance
- Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect rising plasma osmolality and stimulate thirst and release of antidiuretic hormone (ADH, vasopressin). ADH is made in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei and released from the posterior pituitary.
- ADH acts on V2 receptors in the collecting duct, inserting aquaporin-2 channels so water is reabsorbed into the hyperosmotic medulla, producing concentrated urine.
- Without ADH, dilute urine is produced. Diabetes insipidus is caused by lack of ADH (central) or renal unresponsiveness to it (nephrogenic). In the syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion (SIADH), excess ADH causes water retention and low plasma Na⁺.
- Large falls in blood volume also stimulate ADH, and volume can override osmolality.

Sodium balance and ECF volume
- ECF volume depends mainly on total body Na⁺.
- RAAS: renin (from juxtaglomerular cells) converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I; angiotensin-converting enzyme (largely in the lung) makes angiotensin II, which constricts arterioles, increases proximal Na⁺ reabsorption and stimulates aldosterone, ADH and thirst.
- Atrial natriuretic peptide promotes Na⁺ excretion.

Acid–base balance
- Henderson–Hasselbalch: pH = 6.1 + log₁₀([HCO₃⁻]/(0.03 × PCO₂ in mmHg)). Example: HCO₃⁻ 24 mmol/L and PCO₂ 40 mmHg (5.3 kPa) gives 6.1 + log₁₀(20) = 7.40.
- The lungs control PCO₂; the kidneys reclaim filtered bicarbonate and excrete H⁺ (as titratable acid and ammonium), generating new bicarbonate.

Exam tips: be ready to calculate clearance, explain the countercurrent multiplier step by step, and distinguish osmoregulation (ADH and thirst control water) from volume regulation (Na⁺ balance via RAAS).

The gut breaks food into absorbable units, absorbs nutrients, water and electrolytes, and coordinates these processes through nerves and hormones.

Control
- The enteric nervous system: the myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus mainly controls motility; the submucosal (Meissner's) plexus mainly controls secretion and local blood flow.
- Parasympathetic (vagal) input generally stimulates secretion and motility; sympathetic input inhibits them.
- Secretin, discovered by Bayliss and Starling in 1902, is usually described as the first hormone to be identified; Starling introduced the word "hormone" in 1905.

Stomach
- Parietal cells secrete HCl via the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase (proton pump), plus intrinsic factor.
- Acid secretion is stimulated by ACh (vagus, M3 receptors), gastrin (from G cells in the antrum) and histamine (from enterochromaffin-like cells, acting on H2 receptors), and inhibited by somatostatin.
- Chief cells secrete pepsinogen, activated to pepsin by acid.
- Phases of secretion: cephalic (sight, smell and taste via the vagus), gastric (distension and peptides) and intestinal (mainly inhibitory feedback from the duodenum).

Small intestine hormones
- Secretin (S cells): released when acid enters the duodenum; stimulates bicarbonate-rich pancreatic juice.
- Cholecystokinin (CCK, I cells): released in response to fats and amino acids; stimulates gallbladder contraction and pancreatic enzyme secretion and slows gastric emptying.
- GIP and GLP-1: incretins that enhance glucose-stimulated insulin release.

Pancreas and bile
- Pancreatic enzymes are secreted as inactive precursors. Enteropeptidase (enterokinase) on the duodenal brush border activates trypsinogen to trypsin, which activates the other proteases.
- Duct cells secrete bicarbonate via CFTR-dependent Cl⁻ secretion and Cl⁻/HCO₃⁻ exchange, neutralising acid.
- Bile salts emulsify fats and form micelles. About 95% are reabsorbed in the terminal ileum and returned to the liver (enterohepatic circulation).

Carbohydrates
- Starch is digested by salivary and pancreatic amylase; disaccharides by brush-border enzymes (lactase, sucrase-isomaltase, maltase).
- Glucose and galactose enter enterocytes by the Na⁺-glucose cotransporter SGLT1 (secondary active transport driven by the Na⁺ gradient). Fructose enters by facilitated diffusion via GLUT5. All three leave across the basolateral membrane mainly via GLUT2.
- Lactase deficiency leaves lactose in the gut, causing osmotic diarrhoea and fermentation (bloating).

Proteins
- Pepsin, then pancreatic trypsin, chymotrypsin, elastase and carboxypeptidases, then brush-border peptidases.
- Amino acids are absorbed by several Na⁺-coupled transporters; di- and tripeptides by the H⁺-coupled transporter PepT1, then hydrolysed inside the cell.

Fats
- Pancreatic lipase (with colipase) produces monoglycerides and free fatty acids, which travel in micelles to the enterocyte surface.
- Inside, they are re-esterified to triglycerides and packaged with apolipoproteins into chylomicrons, which enter lacteals (lymph) rather than portal blood.
- Fat malabsorption causes steatorrhoea and can lead to deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K).

Vitamin B12 and iron
- B12 binds haptocorrin in the stomach, is released by pancreatic proteases in the duodenum, binds intrinsic factor and is absorbed in the terminal ileum. Loss of intrinsic factor (pernicious anaemia) or ileal disease causes deficiency.
- Iron is absorbed mainly in the duodenum, as Fe²⁺ via DMT1, and leaves the enterocyte through ferroportin. Hepcidin from the liver degrades ferroportin and so limits absorption.

Water and electrolytes
- Several litres of fluid enter the gut daily from food, drink and secretions; most is absorbed in the small intestine and most of the rest in the colon, leaving only a small volume in faeces.
- Water follows solute absorption osmotically. Na⁺ is absorbed by nutrient-coupled transport, Na⁺/H⁺ exchange and, in the distal colon, ENaC.
- Cholera toxin raises cAMP in crypt cells, opening CFTR and causing massive Cl⁻ and water secretion (secretory diarrhoea). Oral rehydration solution works because SGLT1-mediated glucose–Na⁺ cotransport is preserved and drives water absorption.

Motility
- Peristalsis propels contents; segmentation mixes them; the migrating motor complex sweeps the fasting gut.

Exam tips: for each nutrient, trace digestion → brush-border processing → apical transporter → basolateral exit, and link transport physiology to clinical conditions such as cholera, lactose intolerance and pernicious anaemia.

The body must keep blood glucose and core temperature within narrow limits despite intermittent eating and changing environments.

Fed and fasting states
- Fed (absorptive) state: insulin dominates. Glucose is used for energy and stored as glycogen (liver and muscle) and fat; amino acids are used for protein synthesis.
- Fasting (post-absorptive) state: glucagon, adrenaline and cortisol rise. The liver releases glucose by glycogenolysis and then gluconeogenesis (from lactate, glycerol and amino acids such as alanine); adipose tissue releases fatty acids by lipolysis.
- Normal fasting plasma glucose is about 4–6 mmol/L; in the UK a fasting value of 7.0 mmol/L or more is one diagnostic criterion for diabetes.

Insulin
- Secreted by pancreatic β cells. When glucose is taken up and metabolised, the ATP:ADP ratio rises, ATP-sensitive K⁺ channels close, the cell depolarises, voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels open and insulin is released by exocytosis.
- Actions: increases glucose uptake into muscle and adipose tissue (by moving GLUT4 transporters to the membrane), stimulates glycogen, fat and protein synthesis, and inhibits glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, lipolysis and ketogenesis.
- Glucagon (from α cells) acts mainly on the liver to raise glucose: glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis and ketogenesis.

Fuel use and starvation
- Liver glycogen maintains blood glucose for roughly a day of fasting. Muscle glycogen cannot be released as glucose because muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase.
- The brain normally depends on glucose. In prolonged starvation the liver makes ketone bodies (acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate) from fatty acids, and the brain adapts to use them, sparing muscle protein.
- Cori cycle: lactate from muscle and red cells is converted back to glucose in the liver.
- In type 1 diabetes, absolute insulin deficiency allows uncontrolled lipolysis and ketogenesis, which can cause diabetic ketoacidosis.

Energy balance
- Energy content: carbohydrate and protein about 17 kJ/g (4 kcal/g); fat about 37 kJ/g (9 kcal/g); alcohol about 29 kJ/g (7 kcal/g).
- Respiratory quotient (CO₂ produced ÷ O₂ used): about 1.0 for carbohydrate, about 0.7 for fat, about 0.8 for protein.
- Basal metabolic rate is the largest part of daily energy expenditure for most people. Leptin from adipose tissue signals energy stores to the hypothalamus.

Thermoregulation
- Core temperature is kept around 37 °C, with a daily rhythm (lowest in the early morning) and a small rise after ovulation.
- Heat is produced by metabolism, shivering and, especially in infants, non-shivering thermogenesis in brown adipose tissue (uncoupling protein 1 lets mitochondria release energy as heat).
- Heat is lost by radiation, conduction, convection and evaporation. When environmental temperature exceeds skin temperature, evaporation of sweat is the only route of heat loss, so high humidity is dangerous.

Control
- The preoptic area of the anterior hypothalamus integrates information from central and skin thermoreceptors.
- Responses to heat: skin vasodilation (withdrawal of sympathetic vasoconstrictor tone plus active vasodilation, whose transmitter mechanism is not fully understood) and sweating (sympathetic cholinergic fibres acting on muscarinic receptors).
- Responses to cold: skin vasoconstriction (sympathetic, noradrenergic), shivering, non-shivering thermogenesis and behaviour (clothing, shelter).
- Many textbooks describe a hypothalamic "set point". Some physiologists argue instead for a "balance point" arising from several independent effector loops, so this model is debated.

Fever versus hyperthermia
- In fever, pyrogens (e.g. the cytokines IL-1, IL-6 and TNF-α) trigger prostaglandin E₂ production in the hypothalamus, which raises the regulated temperature. The person feels cold and shivers while temperature rises. Antipyretics act by inhibiting cyclo-oxygenase.
- In hyperthermia (e.g. heat stroke), the regulated temperature is unchanged but heat gain overwhelms heat loss. Heat stroke involves a very high core temperature with central nervous system dysfunction.
- Hypothermia is a core temperature below 35 °C. Infants and older people are more vulnerable, through a high surface area to volume ratio and impaired responses respectively.

Exam tips: contrast insulin and glucagon actions organ by organ, explain why muscle glycogen cannot support blood glucose, and distinguish fever (raised regulated temperature) from hyperthermia.

questions.q: If extracellular K⁺ rises from 4 mM to 8 mM (intracellular 140 mM), what happens to E_K at 37 °C?
options: It becomes about 61 mV less negative
It becomes about 18 mV more negative
It becomes about 18 mV less negative
questions.why: Doubling [K⁺]out changes E_K by 61.5 × log₁₀(2) ≈ 18.5 mV, making it less negative (from about −95 to about −76 mV). It cannot become more negative when the outside concentration rises, a 61 mV change would need a tenfold rise, and E_K depends directly on the concentration ratio.

questions.q: What mainly causes repolarisation of a nerve action potential?
options: Na⁺ channel inactivation together with opening of voltage-gated K⁺ channels
questions.why: Repolarisation follows inactivation of voltage-gated Na⁺ channels and delayed opening of voltage-gated K⁺ channels. The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase is far too slow to shape individual action potentials; Cl⁻ channels are not the main mechanism in nerve; and closing K⁺ leak channels would depolarise, not repolarise.

questions.q: Explain why myelinated axons conduct action potentials faster than unmyelinated axons of the same diameter, and give one clinical consequence of demyelination.
markScheme: Myelin increases membrane resistance (less current leak) and decreases capacitance
Longer length constant, so local currents spread further passively
Action potentials generated only at nodes of Ranvier where Na⁺ channels cluster: saltatory conduction
Less charge needed to depolarise each segment; faster and more energy-efficient
Clinical: multiple sclerosis (CNS) or Guillain–Barré (PNS) causing slowed/blocked conduction
questions.modelAnswer: Myelin wraps the axon in many layers of membrane, which greatly increases transmembrane resistance and reduces capacitance. Less current leaks out and less charge is needed to change the membrane potential, so the length constant is longer and local circuit currents spread rapidly and far along the internode. Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels are concentrated at the nodes of Ranvier, so action potentials are regenerated only at the nodes and appear to jump from node to node (saltatory conduction). This is faster and uses less energy, because less Na⁺ enters and must be pumped out. If myelin is damaged, current leaks across the internode and the next node may not reach threshold, slowing or blocking conduction. In multiple sclerosis (central demyelination) this causes symptoms such as visual loss from optic neuritis, and in Guillain–Barré syndrome (peripheral) it causes ascending weakness.

questions.q: Which receptor mediates the effect of postganglionic parasympathetic nerves on the heart?
questions.why: Postganglionic parasympathetic (vagal) fibres release ACh onto M2 muscarinic receptors on the SA and AV nodes, slowing the heart. Nicotinic receptors are found in ganglia and at the NMJ, β1 receptors mediate sympathetic effects on the heart, and α1 receptors mediate mainly vasoconstriction.

questions.q: A patient has weakness that briefly improves with repeated muscle contraction, and a lung tumour. The most likely target of autoantibodies is:
questions.why: This is Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome, often associated with small-cell lung cancer. Antibodies against presynaptic Ca²⁺ channels reduce ACh release, and repeated activity lets Ca²⁺ build up, briefly improving strength. Antibodies to nicotinic receptors cause myasthenia gravis, where weakness worsens with use; acetylcholinesterase and ryanodine receptors are not the usual targets.

questions.q: Describe the sequence of events at the neuromuscular junction from arrival of a motor nerve action potential to generation of a muscle action potential, and explain how acetylcholinesterase inhibitors help in myasthenia gravis.
markScheme: Nerve action potential opens presynaptic voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels; Ca²⁺ influx
SNARE-mediated vesicle fusion; quantal ACh release
ACh binds nicotinic receptors; cation channels open; end-plate potential
EPP exceeds threshold (safety factor); voltage-gated Na⁺ channels; muscle action potential
AChE inhibitors prolong ACh in the cleft, increasing EPP despite fewer receptors in myasthenia
questions.modelAnswer: When the action potential reaches the motor nerve terminal, voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels open and Ca²⁺ flows in. Ca²⁺ triggers SNARE-mediated fusion of synaptic vesicles, releasing many quanta of ACh into the cleft. ACh diffuses across and binds nicotinic receptors on the motor end-plate. These ligand-gated cation channels allow Na⁺ in and K⁺ out, producing a depolarising end-plate potential. Normally the EPP far exceeds the threshold (a high safety factor), so voltage-gated Na⁺ channels in the surrounding muscle membrane open and an action potential propagates along the fibre. ACh is rapidly hydrolysed by acetylcholinesterase. In myasthenia gravis, autoantibodies reduce the number of functional nicotinic receptors, so the EPP may fail to reach threshold, especially with repeated use. Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors slow ACh breakdown, so ACh stays in the cleft longer and activates the remaining receptors repeatedly, restoring the EPP above threshold.

questions.q: In smooth muscle, the Ca²⁺-binding protein that initiates contraction is:
questions.why: In smooth muscle, Ca²⁺ binds calmodulin, which activates myosin light-chain kinase. Troponin C is the Ca²⁺ sensor in skeletal and cardiac muscle, tropomyosin blocks myosin-binding sites on actin but does not bind Ca²⁺ to start contraction, and phospholamban regulates SR Ca²⁺ uptake in the heart.

questions.q: During an isotonic contraction of skeletal muscle, which of the following remains constant in length?
questions.why: The A band corresponds to the length of the thick filaments, which do not change. The I band and H zone shorten as filaments slide past each other, and the sarcomere itself shortens.

questions.q: Compare excitation–contraction coupling in skeletal and cardiac muscle and explain why cardiac muscle cannot be tetanised.
markScheme: Skeletal: T-tubule DHP receptors mechanically coupled to RyR1; Ca²⁺ release does not need Ca²⁺ entry
Cardiac: Ca²⁺ entry through L-type channels triggers Ca²⁺-induced Ca²⁺ release via RyR2
Both: Ca²⁺ binds troponin C; relaxation by SERCA (cardiac also Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchange)
Cardiac contractility can be modulated by altering Ca²⁺ entry (e.g. sympathetic)
Long plateau → long refractory period lasting nearly as long as contraction → no summation/tetanus
questions.modelAnswer: In skeletal muscle, the action potential travels down the T-tubules, where dihydropyridine receptors act as voltage sensors. They are mechanically linked to ryanodine receptors (RyR1) on the sarcoplasmic reticulum, so depolarisation directly opens them and Ca²⁺ is released without needing extracellular Ca²⁺ entry. In cardiac muscle, Ca²⁺ enters through L-type channels during the plateau of the action potential and triggers further Ca²⁺ release through RyR2: Ca²⁺-induced Ca²⁺ release. Because the trigger depends on Ca²⁺ entry, cardiac force can be graded by changing it, for example by sympathetic stimulation. In both, Ca²⁺ binds troponin C to allow cross-bridge cycling, and relaxation depends on Ca²⁺ re-uptake by SERCA (in the heart also extrusion by Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchange). Cardiac muscle cannot be tetanised because the plateau makes the absolute refractory period last nearly as long as the contraction, so a second action potential cannot occur until the muscle has largely relaxed. This ensures the ventricles refill between beats.

questions.q: A patient has heart rate 80 beats/min, end-diastolic volume 140 mL and end-systolic volume 70 mL. What are the cardiac output and ejection fraction?
questions.why: Stroke volume = 140 − 70 = 70 mL; CO = 80 × 70 = 5,600 mL/min = 5.6 L/min; EF = 70/140 = 50%. 11.2 L/min uses the EDV instead of stroke volume; 100% and 200% come from dividing the wrong volumes.

questions.q: Which ionic current is chiefly responsible for the upstroke of the sinoatrial node action potential?
options: Inward Na⁺ current through fast voltage-gated Na⁺ channels
Inward Ca²⁺ current through L-type channels
questions.why: The SA node upstroke is produced by L-type Ca²⁺ channels, which is why it is slow. Fast Na⁺ channels produce the upstroke in atrial and ventricular muscle, I_f contributes to the slow pacemaker depolarisation before threshold, and outward K⁺ current repolarises the cell.

questions.q: State the Frank–Starling law of the heart, explain its cellular basis, and explain its physiological importance.
markScheme: Statement: increased end-diastolic volume/stretch → increased force of contraction and stroke volume
Cellular basis: more optimal actin–myosin overlap at longer sarcomere lengths
Length-dependent increase in myofilament Ca²⁺ sensitivity
Importance: matches output of right and left ventricles beat to beat
Importance: matches cardiac output to venous return (e.g. posture, exercise)
questions.modelAnswer: The Frank–Starling law states that the more the ventricle is filled in diastole (greater end-diastolic volume or preload), the more forcefully it contracts, so stroke volume rises. At the cellular level, cardiac sarcomeres at rest are shorter than optimal, so stretching them improves the overlap between actin and myosin filaments. Stretch also increases the sensitivity of the myofilaments to Ca²⁺ (length-dependent activation), so more force develops at the same Ca²⁺ level. The mechanism matters because it automatically matches the outputs of the two ventricles: if the right ventricle briefly pumps more, the extra blood reaching the left ventricle stretches it and increases its output, preventing blood building up in the lungs. It also matches cardiac output to venous return, for example when venous return rises during exercise or falls on standing.

questions.q: If the radius of an arteriole halves while other factors stay constant, how does its resistance change?
questions.why: By Poiseuille's law resistance is proportional to 1/r⁴, so halving r increases resistance by 2⁴ = 16. Doubling and fourfold increases underestimate the fourth-power dependence, and resistance cannot fall when the vessel narrows.

questions.q: Immediately after a person stands up from lying down, which change is mediated by the baroreceptor reflex?
options: Increased vagal outflow to the SA node
Increased heart rate and peripheral vasoconstriction
questions.why: On standing, venous pooling reduces stroke volume and arterial pressure. Reduced baroreceptor firing increases sympathetic and decreases vagal outflow, raising heart rate and resistance. Decreased sympathetic and increased vagal outflow are the response to a rise in pressure, and ANP is released by atrial stretch, which falls on standing.

questions.q: A patient with liver cirrhosis has a low plasma albumin. Using Starling forces, explain why oedema develops, and list two other mechanisms of oedema with an example of each.
markScheme: Net filtration = K_f[(P_c − P_i) − σ(π_c − π_i)]
Low albumin lowers plasma oncotic pressure (π_c), reducing the force that retains fluid in capillaries
Filtration exceeds lymphatic capacity → interstitial fluid accumulates
Raised capillary hydrostatic pressure, e.g. heart failure or venous obstruction
Increased permeability (inflammation) or lymphatic obstruction (e.g. after node removal)
questions.modelAnswer: Fluid movement across capillaries is governed by Starling forces: net filtration = K_f[(P_c − P_i) − σ(π_c − π_i)]. Plasma proteins, mainly albumin, generate the plasma oncotic pressure that opposes filtration. In cirrhosis the liver makes less albumin, so plasma oncotic pressure falls and the balance shifts towards filtration. When filtration exceeds the ability of lymphatics to return fluid, interstitial fluid accumulates as oedema (and in cirrhosis, portal hypertension also contributes to ascites). Other mechanisms are: raised capillary hydrostatic pressure, as in congestive heart failure or deep vein thrombosis; increased capillary permeability, as in inflammation, where protein leaks and raises interstitial oncotic pressure; and lymphatic obstruction, as after surgical removal of lymph nodes.

questions.q: A person breathes 15 times a minute with a tidal volume of 400 mL and an anatomical dead space of 150 mL. What is their alveolar ventilation?
questions.why: Alveolar ventilation = (400 − 150) × 15 = 3,750 mL/min = 3.75 L/min. 6.0 L/min is total minute ventilation, 2.25 L/min is dead-space ventilation, and 8.25 L/min adds rather than subtracts the dead space.

questions.q: Which change shifts the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve to the left?
questions.why: Cooling increases Hb affinity for O₂, shifting the curve left. Raised PCO₂, raised 2,3-BPG and lower pH (the Bohr effect) all reduce affinity and shift the curve right, helping O₂ unloading in active tissues.

questions.q: Explain how breathing is controlled by arterial PCO₂ and PO₂, identifying the receptors involved.
markScheme: Central chemoreceptors near ventral medulla respond to CSF H⁺
CO₂ crosses blood–brain barrier, forms H⁺; so central receptors track arterial PCO₂; dominant drive at rest
Peripheral chemoreceptors: carotid bodies (IX) and aortic bodies (X)
Peripheral receptors respond to low PaO₂ (marked below ~8 kPa), plus raised PCO₂ and H⁺; only hypoxic sensors
Integration in brainstem respiratory centres alters rate and depth
questions.modelAnswer: Breathing is driven by rhythm-generating neurons in the medulla, modulated by the pons, and adjusted by chemoreceptor input. Central chemoreceptors near the ventral surface of the medulla respond to H⁺ in the cerebrospinal fluid. CO₂ crosses the blood–brain barrier freely and forms H⁺ (via carbonic acid), so these receptors effectively track arterial PCO₂, and they provide most of the normal drive: a small rise in PaCO₂ greatly increases ventilation. Peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid bodies (glossopharyngeal nerve) and aortic bodies (vagus) respond to low arterial PO₂, mainly when it falls below about 8 kPa, as well as to raised PCO₂ and H⁺. They are the only receptors that sense hypoxia, and they respond rapidly to metabolic acidosis. Signals from both sets are integrated in the brainstem to change the rate and depth of breathing, keeping PaCO₂ close to 5.3 kPa.

questions.q: A substance has plasma concentration 2 mg/mL, urine concentration 100 mg/mL and urine flow 1.5 mL/min. GFR is 125 mL/min. What is its clearance, and what does this suggest?
questions.why: Clearance = (100 × 1.5)/2 = 75 mL/min, which is less than GFR (125 mL/min), so (if freely filtered) the substance undergoes net reabsorption. Net secretion would give clearance above GFR; 125 mL/min would match inulin; 300 mL/min comes from multiplying by the plasma concentration (100 × 1.5 × 2) instead of dividing by it.

questions.q: Where does antidiuretic hormone (ADH) mainly act to increase water reabsorption?
options: Collecting duct, via V2 receptors and aquaporin-2
questions.why: ADH binds V2 receptors on collecting duct principal cells and inserts aquaporin-2 channels, allowing water to be reabsorbed into the hyperosmotic medulla. Proximal water reabsorption is not ADH-regulated, the thick ascending limb is impermeable to water, and ADH does not act mainly by changing filtration.

questions.q: Explain how the loop of Henle generates a hyperosmotic medullary interstitium, and how this allows the production of concentrated urine.
markScheme: Thick ascending limb actively reabsorbs NaCl (NKCC2) but is impermeable to water
Creates a horizontal osmotic gradient (~200 mOsm/kg) at each level
Descending limb permeable to water: fluid equilibrates and becomes more concentrated as it descends
Flow multiplies the gradient along the loop: countercurrent multiplication (up to ~1,200 mOsm/kg)
Urea recycling adds to medullary osmolality; vasa recta countercurrent exchange preserves it
ADH makes collecting duct water-permeable (aquaporin-2) so water leaves into hyperosmotic medulla → concentrated urine
questions.modelAnswer: The thick ascending limb actively reabsorbs NaCl through the Na⁺–K⁺–2Cl⁻ cotransporter (NKCC2) but is impermeable to water. This makes the interstitium hyperosmotic relative to fluid in the ascending limb, with a horizontal difference of about 200 mOsm/kg at each level. The descending limb is permeable to water, so water leaves it and its fluid becomes more concentrated as it moves down towards the tip. Because fluid flows in opposite directions in the two limbs, this single effect is multiplied along the length of the loop (countercurrent multiplication), producing a gradient from about 300 mOsm/kg in the cortex to up to about 1,200 mOsm/kg at the papillary tip in humans. Urea recycling between the inner medullary collecting duct and the interstitium adds further osmolality. The vasa recta act as countercurrent exchangers, so blood flow does not wash out the gradient. Fluid leaving the loop is dilute. When ADH is present, aquaporin-2 channels are inserted into the collecting duct, so as the fluid passes through the increasingly hyperosmotic medulla, water leaves by osmosis and urine can become nearly as concentrated as the papillary interstitium.

questions.q: Which hormone is released from duodenal S cells in response to acid and stimulates bicarbonate-rich pancreatic secretion?
questions.why: Secretin is released by acid in the duodenum and stimulates bicarbonate secretion to neutralise it. Gastrin from G cells stimulates gastric acid; CCK from I cells responds to fats and amino acids and mainly stimulates enzyme secretion and gallbladder contraction; somatostatin is generally inhibitory.

questions.q: Why does oral rehydration solution contain glucose as well as salt?
options: Glucose is absorbed with Na⁺ by SGLT1, and water follows osmotically
Glucose provides energy to repair damaged villi
Glucose blocks the cholera toxin receptor
questions.why: SGLT1 cotransports Na⁺ with glucose, and this route stays intact in secretory diarrhoea, so glucose drives Na⁺ and water absorption. Glucose does not block the toxin's receptor or inhibit CFTR, and its role in ORS is to drive absorption rather than supply energy for repair.

questions.q: Describe the digestion and absorption of dietary fat, and explain why disease of the terminal ileum can cause fat malabsorption.
markScheme: Emulsification by bile salts; pancreatic lipase with colipase → monoglycerides and free fatty acids
Micelles carry products to brush border; diffusion/transport into enterocyte
Re-esterification to triglycerides; chylomicrons with apolipoproteins; exit into lacteals/lymph
Bile salts reabsorbed in terminal ileum (enterohepatic circulation, ~95%)
Ileal disease → bile salt loss → reduced pool → poor micelle formation → steatorrhoea (and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency)
questions.modelAnswer: Dietary fat is mainly triglyceride. In the duodenum, bile salts emulsify fat droplets, increasing the surface area. Pancreatic lipase, anchored at the droplet surface by colipase, hydrolyses triglycerides to 2-monoglycerides and free fatty acids. These products, with bile salts and phospholipids, form micelles that carry them through the unstirred water layer to the brush border, where they enter enterocytes. Inside the cells they are re-esterified to triglycerides and packaged with cholesterol, phospholipid and apolipoproteins into chylomicrons. Chylomicrons are too large to enter blood capillaries, so they pass into lacteals and reach the blood via the thoracic duct. About 95% of bile salts are reabsorbed in the terminal ileum and recycled by the liver (enterohepatic circulation). If the terminal ileum is diseased or removed, for example in Crohn's disease, bile salts are lost in the faeces faster than the liver can replace them. The bile salt pool shrinks, micelle formation fails, and fat malabsorption (steatorrhoea) and deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins can result.

questions.q: Which of the following is an action of insulin?
options: Stimulating translocation of GLUT4 to the plasma membrane in skeletal muscle
questions.why: Insulin increases glucose uptake into muscle and fat by moving GLUT4 to the membrane. Gluconeogenesis, lipolysis and ketogenesis are inhibited by insulin and stimulated in the fasting state by glucagon and other counter-regulatory hormones.

questions.q: During a fever, before the temperature reaches its new level, a patient shivers and feels cold. Why?
options: Prostaglandin E₂ directly causes muscle contraction
The hypothalamic regulated temperature has been raised above the current core temperature
Core temperature has fallen below normal
questions.why: Pyrogens increase hypothalamic prostaglandin E₂, raising the regulated temperature, so the current temperature is sensed as too low and heat-gain responses (shivering, vasoconstriction, feeling cold) are triggered. Failure of heat loss describes hyperthermia, prostaglandin E₂ acts centrally rather than directly on muscle, and core temperature is rising, not below normal.

questions.q: Describe how blood glucose is maintained during an overnight fast and during prolonged starvation.
markScheme: Falling insulin and rising glucagon (plus adrenaline, cortisol) in fasting
Overnight: hepatic glycogenolysis is main source; gluconeogenesis increasing
Muscle glycogen cannot supply blood glucose (no glucose-6-phosphatase)
Prolonged: glycogen exhausted; gluconeogenesis from amino acids, lactate, glycerol; lipolysis supplies fatty acids
Ketogenesis; brain adapts to ketones, sparing protein
questions.modelAnswer: After an overnight fast, insulin secretion falls and glucagon rises (with contributions from adrenaline and cortisol). Glucagon acts on the liver to break down glycogen (glycogenolysis), which is the main source of blood glucose at this stage, while gluconeogenesis begins to increase. Muscle glycogen cannot supply blood glucose because muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase; it is used locally. Fatty acids released from adipose tissue by lipolysis become the main fuel for muscle, sparing glucose for the brain and red cells. In prolonged starvation, liver glycogen is exhausted within roughly a day, and glucose comes entirely from gluconeogenesis using amino acids (from muscle protein), lactate (Cori cycle) and glycerol. The liver converts fatty acids into ketone bodies (acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate). Over days the brain adapts to use ketones for much of its energy, which reduces glucose demand and so spares muscle protein.

questions.q: Essay: Describe the mechanisms that regulate arterial blood pressure in the short and long term. Illustrate your answer with the body's response to a haemorrhage of about 1 litre.
markScheme: Framework: MAP = CO × TPR; CO = HR × SV; determinants of each
Baroreceptor reflex: receptors, afferents (IX, X), NTS, efferent sympathetic/vagal effects on HR, contractility, arterioles, veins
Baroreceptor resetting; role mainly short-term
Long-term: renal pressure natriuresis; RAAS (stimuli and actions of angiotensin II, aldosterone); ADH; ANP
Haemorrhage immediate: fall in venous return/SV/MAP → baroreflex tachycardia, vasoconstriction, venoconstriction; preservation of cerebral/coronary flow
Haemorrhage intermediate: capillary fluid shift (Starling), RAAS, ADH, thirst
Haemorrhage late: hepatic plasma protein synthesis, erythropoietin-driven red cell replacement
Integration and clear structure; local autoregulation mentioned
questions.modelAnswer:
Mean arterial pressure (MAP) is approximately cardiac output (CO) multiplied by total peripheral resistance (TPR), and CO is heart rate multiplied by stroke volume. Regulation therefore acts on heart rate, contractility, venous return and arteriolar tone, and in the long run on blood volume.

Short-term control is dominated by the arterial baroreceptor reflex. Stretch receptors in the carotid sinus (glossopharyngeal nerve) and aortic arch (vagus) fire in proportion to pressure and project to the nucleus tractus solitarius in the medulla. A fall in pressure reduces their firing, which increases sympathetic outflow and decreases vagal outflow. Heart rate rises (via β1 receptors on the SA node and less M2 activity), contractility increases, arterioles constrict (α1), raising TPR, and veins constrict, shifting blood centrally to support venous return and, by the Frank–Starling mechanism, stroke volume. The reflex acts within seconds but resets if pressure changes persist, so it mainly buffers short-term changes. Local autoregulation keeps flow to the brain, heart and kidneys fairly constant over a range of pressures.

Long-term control depends on the kidney's control of extracellular volume. Raised pressure increases Na⁺ and water excretion (pressure natriuresis). Reduced renal perfusion, sympathetic β1 stimulation and low NaCl at the macula densa release renin. Angiotensin II then constricts arterioles, increases proximal Na⁺ reabsorption, and stimulates aldosterone (Na⁺ reabsorption via ENaC), ADH and thirst. Atrial natriuretic peptide opposes these when volume is high.

After a 1 litre haemorrhage, venous return, stroke volume and MAP fall. Within seconds the baroreflex produces tachycardia, cool, pale skin from vasoconstriction, and reduced gut and renal blood flow, while cerebral and coronary flow are preserved. Over minutes to hours, arteriolar constriction lowers capillary hydrostatic pressure, so Starling forces favour fluid entering capillaries from the interstitium, partly restoring plasma volume. Renin, angiotensin II, aldosterone and ADH reduce Na⁺ and water excretion, and thirst increases intake. Over days to weeks, the liver replaces plasma proteins and erythropoietin from the kidney stimulates red cell production. Together, fast neural and slower renal and hormonal mechanisms restore pressure and then volume.

questions.q: Essay: How does the body maintain the osmolality and volume of its body fluids? Include the role of the kidney, and explain what happens when ADH secretion is absent or excessive.
markScheme: Compartments: TBW ~60%, ICF/ECF split; osmolality ~285–295 mOsm/kg; Na⁺ determines ECF volume
Osmoregulation: hypothalamic osmoreceptors → ADH (supraoptic/paraventricular, posterior pituitary) and thirst
ADH action: V2 receptors, aquaporin-2, collecting duct; depends on medullary gradient (countercurrent multiplication, urea, vasa recta)
Volume regulation: baroreceptors and renal sensors; RAAS (renin stimuli, angiotensin II, aldosterone/ENaC); ANP; pressure natriuresis
Interaction: volume depletion can stimulate ADH and override osmolality
ADH absence: diabetes insipidus (central vs nephrogenic): large volumes of dilute urine, thirst, risk of hypernatraemia
ADH excess: SIADH: water retention, concentrated urine, dilutional hyponatraemia
Clear distinction between water (osmolality) and Na⁺ (volume) control
questions.modelAnswer:
In a 70 kg adult about 60% of body weight is water, two-thirds intracellular and one-third extracellular. Water moves freely between compartments, so all share an osmolality of about 285–295 mOsm/kg. Because Na⁺ is the main extracellular solute and is largely excluded from cells, total body Na⁺ determines extracellular fluid (ECF) volume, while water balance determines osmolality. The body therefore uses two related but distinct control systems.

Osmolality is regulated by water intake and excretion. Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect small rises in plasma osmolality and stimulate thirst and secretion of ADH (vasopressin), which is made in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei and released from the posterior pituitary. ADH binds V2 receptors on collecting duct principal cells, raising cAMP and inserting aquaporin-2 channels into the luminal membrane. Water then moves by osmosis into the hyperosmotic medullary interstitium. That gradient is created by countercurrent multiplication in the loop of Henle (NaCl reabsorption by NKCC2 in the water-impermeable thick ascending limb), urea recycling, and countercurrent exchange in the vasa recta. Urine can range from very dilute to about four times plasma osmolality.

Volume is regulated mainly through Na⁺ excretion. Falls in effective circulating volume are sensed by arterial baroreceptors, atrial stretch receptors and the kidney. Renin is released in response to reduced renal perfusion pressure, sympathetic β1 stimulation and reduced NaCl delivery to the macula densa. Angiotensin II increases proximal Na⁺ reabsorption, constricts arterioles and stimulates aldosterone, which increases Na⁺ reabsorption through ENaC in the collecting duct, and it also stimulates ADH and thirst. Atrial natriuretic peptide, released by atrial stretch, promotes Na⁺ excretion, and pressure natriuresis links arterial pressure to Na⁺ output. A large fall in volume also releases ADH and can override osmotic control.

If ADH is absent (central diabetes insipidus) or the kidney cannot respond (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus), the collecting duct stays impermeable to water, so large volumes of dilute urine are passed. Patients are very thirsty and become hypernatraemic if they cannot drink enough. If ADH is secreted in excess, as in the syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion, water is retained and urine is inappropriately concentrated. Plasma Na⁺ falls by dilution, while the body corrects volume by excreting Na⁺, so patients are typically euvolaemic with hyponatraemia.
